Here is the part nobody tells you about a pause. After about two seconds of silence, the person listening stops thinking about your topic and starts guessing why you stopped. And the guess is almost never the true reason. You are looking for a word, and they have decided you do not know the answer, or that you are hiding something, or that you did not understand the question. That is the whole cost, and it happens in two seconds. Now, people always ask me whether the fix is to speak faster. It is not, and speaking faster usually makes it worse, because the problem was never your speed. The problem is the gap. So you fill the gap out loud, with a sentence that says what you are doing. That is a good question. Let me think about that for a second. There are two things here. None of those sentences has any content at all, and every one of them keeps the listener with you. And one more thing, which is the one I care about most. Never apologise for pausing. The apology costs more than the pause did. Nobody had noticed until you said sorry, and from that moment on, everybody in the room is waiting for the next one.

I went completely blank in an interview two years ago, and the funny part is which question did it. It was not a hard one. It was why did you choose this course, which is the most predictable question in the world, and I had rehearsed the difficult ones and never once said that answer out loud. So I sat there for about four seconds, which felt like a week, and then I apologised, which made it worse. What I do now is very simple and it took me about a year to learn. In the first two seconds of every answer I say one sentence before I have decided anything at all. Usually that is a good question, or there are two things here, and I genuinely do not know the two things yet when I say it. The rest arrives while I am talking. That is the part that surprised me: the thinking does not have to happen before the talking. And I still rehearse, but only the first thirty seconds of an answer and nothing after it, because a memorised answer falls apart the moment somebody asks the follow-up question, and there is always a follow-up question.
